title: Ceeb bu Weex
localName: Ceeb bu weex — thièb bou wekh, thieboudiene blanc
author: Aïssatou Mbaye
desc: The white ceebu jen — made without tomato, distinguished by a sorrel sauce called beuguedj and by the soul, a fish-free ball of pounded nététou.
longDesc: Not plain rice, and the distinction matters: this is a ceebu jen cooked in broth without tomato, and it has two features the red version does not. The beuguedj is a sauce of white bissap sorrel leaves. The soul is a ball made with néré and nététou — fermented locust bean — containing no fish at all, buried in the rice to finish. About twenty centilitres of oil, roughly two litres of water, and an hour's simmer. The rice is washed three times to reduce the starch. Her own verdict is that it needs patience and care, and that it is one of her favourites.
ingredients: // Quantities printed only inside the method; see the note
White bissap sorrel leaves — quantity not printed
Cherry tomatoes, crushed — quantity not printed
// For the soul: néré and nététou, pounded into a ball — quantities not printed
steps: Crush the cherry tomatoes. Dice the onion and half the bell pepper, and cut a chilli in two.
Put the pot on the heat with about 20 cl of oil.
Add the onion, pepper and cut chilli, the yett and the crushed tomatoes, and fry until you get a brown colour.
When the pot comes to the boil, add the vegetables and the white bissap, cover, and cook.
Pound the roff — parsley, 2 or 3 bird's eye chillies, 3 cloves of garlic, pepper and a little salt.
Make a hole in the flesh of the fish and stuff it with the roff, then add the fish to the pot.
Pound or chop the nokoss — onion, garlic, a handful of nététou, chillies, half a bell pepper, bouillon if using, and salt.
Add part of the nokoss and the prawns, cover, and let it simmer for 1 hour.
After the hour, wash the rice 3 times to reduce the starch.
Remove the vegetables and fish to a large bowl, add the tamarind and a ladle of broth.
Cook the rice in the remaining broth.
// The soul, a ball of pounded néré and nététou with no fish in it, is served with the dish.
chefTips: Without tomato is the whole point. It is not unseasoned rice — one source glosses the name specifically as not to be confused with plain rice — it is rice cooked in a seasoned fish broth.
Fry the base until you get a brown colour. That browning is where the dish's depth comes from in the absence of tomato.
Wash the rice three times, by her instruction, to reduce the starch. In a dish this brothy, loose starch is what turns it claggy.
The soul is the unusual element — a pounded ball of néré and nététou with no fish in it at all. It is the fermented-bean counterpart to the fish stuffing.
Beuguedj, the white-sorrel sauce, is the other thing that marks the white version. White bissap, not the red hibiscus used for drinks.

Be aware the source prints no formal ingredient list — only the quantities that appear inside the method. Several ingredients are named without any amount, and this entry says so rather than inventing figures.
Her own framing: it requires patience and care. An hour's simmer before the rice even goes in.
commonMistakes: Treating it as plain white rice.
Skipping the browning stage, which leaves it flat.
Washing the rice once rather than three times.
Leaving out the soul, which is most of what makes it the white version.
Using red hibiscus in place of white bissap.
sources: Adapted from 'Ceeb bu weex, thièb bou wekh ou thieboudiene blanc', aistoucuisine.com — the page title appends ' - Aistou Cuisine'. BYLINE: Aïssatou Mbaye. Date: 9 mai 2016. Number of servings: NOT STATED, absent. TWO-PASS on everything reported.

A SUBSTANTIAL GAP, stated plainly: NO FORMAL INGREDIENT LIST IS PRINTED. Quantities exist only inside the method, and only these are printed — 'environ 20 cl d'huile'; 'Ajouter environ 2 litres d'eau'; for the roff '2 ou 3 piments oiseau', '3 gousses d'ail', 'du poivre et un peu de sel'; for the nokoss '1 oignon', '2 gousses d'ail', 'une poignée de nététou', '2 piments oiseau', '1/2 poivron', 'un bouillon cube (si vous souhaitez)', 'du sel'; and for the rice, 'laver le riz 3 fois pour réduire l'amidon'. NAMED WITHOUT QUANTITIES, and no figures are invented for them: poisson, crevettes, légumes, bissap blanc, tomates cerises, yett, persil, tamarin, and the onion, pepper and chilli for the rissolé. The six servings above is editorial.

THE ONLY TWO DONENESS CUES PRINTED, in French as printed: 'jusqu'à obtenir une couleur brune' for the rissolé, and 'Lorsque la marmite est en ébullition'. The one explicit time is 'laisser mijoter pendant 1 heure'. The covered vegetable cook carries NO time — absent. No temperatures anywhere.

LOCAL VOCABULARY AS PRINTED, recorded because this entry is the best glossary in the Senegalese material: Ceeb bu weex, thièb bou wekh (thiébou wekh), thieboudiene / thieboudienne, beuguedj (also written 'béguète' in the MAGGI printing at SEN005), soul, nététou (netetou, 'aussi appelé Soumbala'), néré (Parkia biglobosa), roff, yett, bissap blanc, nokoss, piment oiseau.

THE AUTHOR'S OWN FRAMING OF RED VERSUS WHITE: she presents this as a variation on the red thieboudiene, MADE WITHOUT TOMATO, with largely the same method, distinguished by the beuguedj sorrel sauce and by the soul, a fish-free ball made with néré and nététou. She calls it one of her favourites, says it requires patience and care, and describes it as embodying Senegalese cuisine, 'flavourful and full of character'.

HOW WELL ATTESTED THE WHITE VERSION ACTUALLY IS — and the database should not imply parity with the red. The red version has four independent printings in this collection. For the white: this entry and SEN005 are the only two sources with usable method detail, and the TERMINOLOGY itself is attested separately just once, SINGLE-PASS, in 'La cuisine Sénégalaise : Art culinaire de l'Afrique de l'Ouest!', afrik.com, BYLINE AS PRINTED 'Florence' (first name only), 'Publié le 22 octobre 2011 à 14h32', which prints '«Tieb bou khonkh» (riz rouge)' and '«Tieb bou weikh» (riz blanc, à ne pas confondre avec riz nature)'. That parenthetical gloss — not to be confused with plain rice — is the single most useful sentence found on the white version and is why this entry's description leads with it. NOTE the spellings there are 'Tieb bou khonkh' and 'Tieb bou weikh', not the 'bu xonq' / 'bu weex' used elsewhere.

CONFIRMED ABSENT, across two passes: the UNESCO nomination file does NOT use the red/white distinction at all, nor does the English Representative List page, nor three of the four red-version printings consulted.

A RETRIEVAL NOTE WORTH RECORDING for anyone rebuilding this: an earlier research round against aistoucuisine.com found the ingredient list and method step 1 ABSENT from the fetched text on every page across both passes, on six URLs — the site is JavaScript-rendered. A later round recovered the figures by asking for structured data extraction ('list every ingredient with its exact printed quantity as a separate item; do not paraphrase the numbers') rather than verbatim transcription. That framing is what made this author usable at all.
reheating: Steam the rice; warm the fish and vegetables in broth.
healthBenefits: Nététou is high in protein and its alkaline fermentation improves amino-acid availability.
Sorrel leaves contribute vitamin C and organic acids.
No tomato, so suitable for those avoiding nightshade acidity.
High in protein from fish and prawns together.
culturalNote: That Senegal has a white ceebu jen at all surprises people who only know the red one, and it is the older-feeling dish — no tomato, which arrived late, and a fermented locust-bean ball at its centre. The soul is the detail to notice: a fish-free element in a fish dish, there for the ferment rather than the protein.
